question: Is Loeys-Dietz syndrome inherited ?
references: Loeys-Dietz syndrome is considered to have an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, which means one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder.  In about 75 percent of cases, this disorder results from a new gene mutation and occurs in people with no history of the disorder in their family. In other cases, an affected person inherits the mutation from one affected parent.
greedy_answer:
Yes, Loeys-Dietz syndrome is an inherited disorder. It is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder, which means that a mutation in one of the two copies of the gene is sufficient to cause the condition. 

Loeys-Dietz syndrome is caused by mutations in the TGFBR1 or TGFBR2 genes, which are responsible for encoding proteins that play a crucial role in the development and maintenance of the connective tissue. These genes are located on chromosomes 3 (TGFBR2) and 9 (TGFBR1).

If one parent has Loeys-Dietz syndrome, each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutated gene and developing the condition. If both parents are carriers of the mutated gene, each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutated gene and a 50% chance of being a carrier but not having the condition.

It's worth noting that Loeys-Dietz syndrome can also occur spontaneously, without a family history of the condition, due to a de novo mutation. This means that a new mutation occurs in the egg or sperm cell, resulting in a child with the condition without a family history.
